item.title: Should England be charging a tourism tax?
item.description: A well-implemented visitor levy can indeed have a positive effect on the tourism industry but there are many nuances to consider.
item.content:encoded:
Supporters tend to call it a “visitor levy”. Detractors prefer to call it a “tourist tax”.

Whether you agree with it or not, an extra charge for overnight stays has become a common feature of modern travel. Recent visitors to New York, Prague, Milan and Edinburgh will have already paid it. And now mayors in England will have the chance to impose it.

Some think these fees will cause huge damage to the hospitality sector, while adding to the general cost of living for visitors. But the main argument in favour of the charge is that it is a simple way of raising much-needed revenue.

A report I worked on for the Welsh government showed that a well-implemented visitor levy can indeed have a positive effect on the tourism industry.

Looking at destinations in Italy, Iceland, Spain and the US, the evidence suggested that a tourism tax can bring benefits to the local community while also improving sustainability, by funding environmental projects, for example.

But getting it implemented turns out to be far from simple. There are key elements which have to be decided upon, and different places – big cities and coastal towns, for example – need different approaches.

item.title: ‘EC has become dictatorial’: Ex-bureaucrats demand CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation

item.content:encoded:
A group of former bureaucrats on Monday demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar for alleged irregularities in the conduct of special intensive revision of electoral rolls in the country.

In an open letter, the Constitutional Conduct Group said that the Election Commission’s functioning has become “imperious, autocratic and dictatorial” because of Kumar. It added that his actions around the SIR exercise represented “serious infringement” of constitutional functioning and legality.

On Saturday, the group had called on the Election Commission to scrap the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

The letter came amid similar demands by the Opposition and civil society groups for Kumar’s removal over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the poll panel. The demands came after The Indian Express reported on Wednesday that two election commissioners had objected to decisions related to the SIR.

The newspaper’s investigation showed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected 14 times in 10 months to the poll panel’s decisions about the SIR, saying that some had been taken without their knowledge.

item.title: ‘At every turn / street dogs ask with erect ears / ‘Who are you?’: Fifteen haikus about modern life
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Suddenly the Moon’, by Anirudh Acharya.
item.content:encoded:
1

Playing by itself
with an abandoned slipper —

the evening sea

2

In the open night
the attar on my wrist too
smells of the moon

3

Much to say to you
not in front of the others —
my eyes tell the moon

4

She wipes her brow
with the back of her hand —
ãttã in her hair

5

Candlelight dinner
Needing a phone’s light to
Look at the menu

6

The only sign
of autumn’s coming —
“End of Season” sale

7

Suddenly the moon —
out over the vast ocean
rain clouds drifting by

8

In this well-lived home
even by the old kitchen sink
fond memories

9

Deep in the mountains
surrounded by many trees —
joy of learning names

10

Midday at the beach —
lovers snuggle closer-in
quickly shrinking shade

11

Lost to the city
but here in this tiny lane —
chirping of sparrows

12

Again fresh flowers
on the road leading
to the burning ground

13

Sleepy afternoon —
white spots on an orange cat
filled in by sunlight


14

At the beach
people sit facing the sea
to look into phones

15

At every turn
street dogs ask with erect ears
“Who are you?”

item.title: Hardy crops are failing in drought-hit parts of Karnataka
item.description: There has been a decline in ragi and millet kharif sowing area.
item.content:encoded:
Shiva Shekhar, a 40-year-old farmer from Padavalapatna village in Mandya district’s Nagamangala taluk, could not sow ragi this kharif. “I kept waiting for the rain but it never came, so I sowed cowpea instead, which is more drought-tolerant,” he said on September 16.

Karnataka is the largest ragi-producing state in the country. In 2025-’26, India produced 2 million tonnes of ragi, of which 1.47 million tonnes came from Karnataka, according to the Third Advance Estimates for the year from the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The state also accounted for about 73% of the area under ragi that year, at 979,000 hectares. Of that, Mandya –located about 40 km north of Mysuru – accounted for about 53,300 hectares.

Broadly, ragi sowing at the national and state levels has kept pace with last year. But in Mandya, against a target of 63,385 hectare for this year, ragi was sown in 1,213 hectare (1.91%) by September 11, data shared by Jayaswamy, joint director of agriculture for Mandya, show.

By September 11, Karnataka had an overall decline of 1.5 million hectares in kharif sowing area compared to last year. Of this, roughly a third each was in paddy, and the broad category of millets and coarse cereals.

item.title: J&K passes Omar Abdullah’s statehood resolution amid walkout by BJP
item.description: Bharatiya Janata Party MLAs objected to a reference to the 2000 autonomy resolution in the new one.
item.content:encoded:
The Jammu and Kashmir Assembly on Monday passed a resolution, moved by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, seeking statehood for the Union Territory amid protests by Bharatiya Janata Party legislators, The Hindu reported.

While the Congress and the Peoples Democratic Party MLAs supported the move, the BJP legislators shouted slogans against it over its reference to the resolution passed by the Assembly in 2000.

In June 2000, the National Conference government led by Farooq Abdullah passed a resolution in the Assembly calling for restoration of greater autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir as it existed before August 1953. However, it was rejected by the then-Atal Bihari Vajpayee government at the Centre.

The text of the fresh resolution moved by Abdullah on Friday says that in addition to the resolutions passed by the Assembly in June 2000 and November 2024, the House was calling on the Union government to urgently restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood.

In November 2024, the Assembly passed another resolution calling for the restoration of the special status the erstwhile state had under Article 370 of the Constitution, which was abrogated by the Union government in August 2019.

item.title: Fiction: Brothers Cyrus and Rumi will carry their deep-rooted grudges from old Bombay to the new
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Bombay Tabloid’, by Kersi Khambatta.
item.content:encoded:
“Disgusting behaviour,” were the first words Adi Kerman snarled thickly at 7 am when he read the headline of the Indian Express, Mumbai edition, Saturday, April 26, 1997: Businessman Shot Dead in Broad Daylight.

He returned from the bakery earlier than usual that afternoon, a black thundercloud still tethered to his big bullet head. His common-law wife caught the mood, did not probe, and took off on her own to catch the 4 pm show at Ganga Talkies right next door. Adi paced and kicked furniture listlessly, waiting for his son Cyrus to pop in for ritual Saturday sundowners at 6 pm.

“The weather is going nuts,” huffed Cyrus cheerfully, bang on time, airing out a moist, sticky T-shirt as he sank into his designated spot on the vermilion-coloured sofa.

“Wait a month,” Adi snarled. “Then it will be flat-out mental.”

item.title: SC refuses to stay fee on UPI payments above Rs 2,000
item.description: However, the bench asked the Union government to explain the decision to allow the charges.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday refused to stay the Union government’s decision to allow fee to be levied on Unified Payments Interface transactions above Rs 2,000, Live Law reported.

However, the court sought the government’s response on the petition challenging the move.

On September 14 and September 15, the Ministry of Finance issued notifications stating that UPI payments to merchants valued above Rs 2,000 would attract a merchant discount rate of 0.4%.

Merchant discount rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.

The petitioner submitted before the court that businesses may pass on the additional cost of the UPI charges to consumers.

Additional Solicitor General N Venkataraman, appearing for the Union government, submitted before the court that 96% of transactions would not attract the charge, Live Law reported. The charges would take effect on October 15.

“It is neither a tax nor a fee,” he was quoted as saying.

Chief Justice Surya Kant said that the government should place these facts on an affidavit as “it is more of a technical issue”, the legal news outlet reported.

The Supreme Court on Monday took suo moto cognisance of a spate of rape cases in Delhi, saying it underlined a “systematic failure” of the law enforcement authorities and the administration to guarantee basic public safety, Live Law reported.

At least 13 cases of sexual assault have been reported in Delhi this month, The Print reported.

These include the gang rape of a 17-year-old allegedly by three men who posed as police personnel in a park near Lady Shri Ram College on September 21.

On September 13, the body of a 16-year-old girl was found decomposed in Swaroop Nagar, two days after she was allegedly raped and murdered, The Hindu reported.

On August 4, a 17-year-old was gang raped by a bus driver and conductor inside a moving bus as it covered a distance of nearly 47 km from Greater Noida to Kashmere Gate without being checked at any police picket, The Indian Express reported.

On Monday, the bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said that they were distressed by these reports and highlighted the need to fix accountability.

While referring to the August 4 case, the bench said that “one cannot help but draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.

item.title: A new self-help book argues that ‘fake it till you make it’ actually works
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Be Delusional: Bend Reality to Your Beliefs’, by Harinder Singh Pelia.
item.content:encoded:
Has it ever happened to you that you ask someone who they are, and first they give you some random labels, then they start telling you even more random stories? Like, I am a senior manager of random things at Random Pvt. Ltd, and then, the moment you make the mistake of becoming slightly comfortable, they launch into a story of their childhood. Let’s admit it: we’ve all done a version of this at some point. There is a collection of stories we carry within us only to tell other people, but there is also a larger collection we hold to tell ourselves.

Psychologist Dan McAdams has spent all his life figuring out the stories people tell themselves and others. item.title: Uttar Pradesh: 56 killed, 46 injured in floods
item.description: In Odisha, one lakh persons were taken to relief camps because of waterlogging, while 5,000 had been rescued in Chhattisgarh.
item.content:encoded:
Fifty-six persons died and 46 were injured in Uttar Pradesh between Friday and Sunday as heavy rains battered the state, causing flooding and crop loss, reported The Indian Express.

Waterlogging caused by heavy rainfall had also led to more than one lakh persons being moved to relief camps in Odisha. Severe flooding was also reported in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar region.

The toll in Uttar Pradesh from rain-related incidents is expected to rise as officials were compiling the data, state Relief Commissioner Hrishikesh Bhaskar Yashod was quoted as saying by the Hindustan Times.

The state received 66.5 mm of rainfall between Friday and Sunday, against the normal 7.6 mm for the period. Excessive rainfall was recorded in 56 of Uttar Pradesh’s 75 districts.

This led to more than 1,020 houses being damaged and 107 animals dying.

Among the districts, Farrukhabad recorded the highest above-normal rainfall at 7,385%, followed by Kannauj at 5,664%, Shahjahanpur at 4,408%, Hamirpur at 4,240% and Mahoba at 4,100%.

item.title: Beyond the myth of India’s Sanskrit-speaking villages, can the language anchor modern life?
item.description: To truly revitalise a language, it must belong to the messy, everyday realities of its speakers.
item.content:encoded:
For over two decades, an extraordinary cultural and political experiment has unfolded along the mist-shrouded slopes of the Himalayas. The state government of Uttarakhand set out to construct a network of saṃskṛta-grāms – dedicated “Sanskrit-speaking” villages designed to transform the region into a living, breathing Sanskrit wonderland. Crores of rupees were poured into local administrations with a bold vision: resurrecting the “Language of the Gods” from its classical and liturgical repose and embedding it into the soil of everyday rural Indian life.

Yet, year after year, this ambitious policy narrative undergoes a curious ritual of its own.It is repeatedly re-released, temporarily mobilising ideological enthusiasts, only to stall amid bureaucratic quietude and persistent allegations of corruption. Initially promised for every administrative block and district, the actual mapping of operational Sanskrit villages has been drastically reduced to a sparse handful of locations.

As illustrated in Image 1, the state’s sprawling ambitions have contracted to just 13 specific geographic pockets – including Kotgaon in the north, Kimothā and Bhantola in Chamoli, and Nagla Tarai in the far south.

This gap between state-sponsored imagination and institutional reality raises a profound question: Is Sanskrit truly a living, spoken vernacular capable of anchoring modern life, or does its power reside entirely in its function as a mythic...

item.title: True story: In Phoolan Devi and Kusma Nain’s stories, a combustible mix of jealousy and betrayal
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Massacre Queens: True Story Of Love And Revenge In the Chambals’, by Ashwini Bhatnagar.
item.content:encoded:
Vikram Mallah and Babu Gujjar made an odd pair.

Babu Gujjar was a thick-boned, well-muscled man over six feet tall with a large bulbous nose. Sharp crocodile-like teeth sprang forth when he opened his mouth, ready to bite and chew big chunks of flesh. His flowing, shaggy beard often stowed away twigs and little dead leaves of stunted kikar trees in its undergrowth. The hair on his head was equally unruly – it fell in a tangled mess on his forehead, got into his eyes, and billowed around his shoulders with the breeze. Whenever the air around him turned unusually frisky, Babu Gujjar tied a bandana around his head.

The bandana forced attention to his bulging eyes. One was pitch black, while the other was murky white. He had lost his left eye to a childhood injury and was therefore known as Kana Dacait. An obnoxious pall of body odour thickly wrapped itself around him, too.

Babu was a gujjar by caste, hence the Gujjar after his first name. The gujjars, once a nomadic pastoralist community, were historically viewed as marauders. Max (Jamie Foxx) is tempted by the money that Vincent (Tom Cruise) is offering to be driven around Los Angeles for the rest of the night while he takes care of business. item.title: Bastar village looks for truth and reconciliation as Maoist-police strife ends
item.description: Chinnari village’s negotiations offer a glimpse of the messy aftermath of decades-long conflict in the region. The first part in a new series.
item.content:encoded:
Chhinari is a medium-sized village of about 80 households nestled in Chhattisgarh’s Narayanpur district. Most of its residents are Adivasis from the Muria Gond community, while around 13 families belong to the Yadav community.

For two decades, the conflict between Maoist insurgents and the police violently disrupted their lives, bitterly dividing both Adivasi and Yadav families. Now, with the state announcing a victory over the Maoists, the residents of Chhinari are attempting to repair the ruptures in their social fabric and return to an older rhythm of life.

But this was proving to be difficult – or so I heard from local contacts in the area.

One Saturday in June, I decided to find out more by travelling to Chinnari to attend the weekly village meeting where residents gather to discuss matters of common concern.

Around 7 am, when I reached the village, I found both the young and the old were walking down to the meeting point – an open space that once held two Maoist memorials, but is now ringed by a newly built panchayat bhavan, a primary school and a community centre.

item.title: Is calisthenics an effective form of exercise or just another fitness fad?
item.description: Learning to move your own body, control it and gradually make it stronger is one of the simplest, cheapest ways to start training.
item.content:encoded:
Calisthenics has gained enormous popularity in recent years, particularly thanks to social media and the rise of workout areas in city parks. You probably know some of the moves already, like pull-ups, push-ups, dips and squats.

For the more advanced, it also includes eye-catching, gravity-defying moves like the muscle-up, planche (where the body is held horizontal, supported solely by the hands) or the front lever (where the body is held horizontally while hanging from a bar).

But is calisthenics an effective form of exercise, or just another fitness fad? To answer this question, we first need to clarify what it is.

Calisthenics is a form of training that mainly uses a person’s own body weight as resistance. Its name derives from the Greek terms kállos (“beautiful”) and sthenos (“strength”), though the word’s modern use only caught on during the 19th century, when it referred to various forms of physical exercise.

Today, it includes well-known exercises such as squats, lunges, push-ups, pull-ups and dips, but calisthenics is not inherently acrobatic. Anyone who starts by doing a simple wall push-up is using the same principle as someone doing a one-arm push-up on the ground: moving their body against gravity.

item.title: Literary tourism: Why the places we love in books can never quite be found in real life
item.description: Literary geography, which combines physical geography with literary studies, emerged as the novel became popular and grew alongside literary tourism.
item.content:encoded:
From the Brontës’ Haworth to Jane Austen’s Bath, Wordsworth’s Lake District and Thomas Hardy’s Dorset, literary places continue to exert a powerful hold over readers.

Literary tourism appears to be enjoying renewed popularity, from visits inspired by classic novels to the TikTok trend of turning books into travel itineraries. But what exactly are literary tourists hoping to find when they get there? The answer is more complicated than it might seem.

Haworth, Bath and Dorset all exist, obviously. They can be found on a map and visited. But the Brontë moors, Austen’s Bath, Wordsworth’s Lakes and Hardy’s Wessex are also literary reimaginings of those places. They may never have existed in quite the form readers imagine.

Our fascination with literary places has a long history. Literary geography, which combines physical geography with literary studies, emerged in the late 19th century as the novel grew in popularity and, in many ways, grew alongside literary tourism.

In 1899, William Lyon Phelps created his Literary Map of England, marking locations associated with authors and literary works. A few years later, William Sharp’s Literary Geography (1904) mapped regions such as “Dickens land”, “the Brontë country” and the literary geography of the English lakes.

item.title: Google Earth’s disastrous AI image generation experiment shows need for guardrails

This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

Since Israel and the US launched strikes against Iran in February, plunging the Gulf region into conflict, the countries have also been waging an information war using tools powered by artificial intelligence. To separate fact from fiction, authorities, analysts, and journalists alike turned to commercial satellite imagery, including Google Earth, the closest thing to “ground truth,” with limited access to sites.

Google Earth has long been a trusted infrastructure for the verification field, and is the platform on which open-source investigators are formally trained for conflict work in Syria, Yemen, and Sudan. Yet on July 30, Google launched a new feature that built image generation directly into Google Earth, the product that for two decades was synonymous with satellite image truth.

China’s used car dealers have set an expiry date for electric cars.

About four out of five used car dealers in China refuse to accept a fully electric vehicle older than five years, over worries about battery life and replacement costs, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook. A three-year-old EV in China now resells for about 45% of its original price, down from almost 55% in 2023, according to the China Automobile Dealers Association.

China has been the world’s largest EV market for a decade and now has 44 million of them on its roads. This makes it the first country where EVs are aging in large numbers. The countries that have imported Chinese EVs will face the same valuation problem as the cars turn five.

item.title: Instead of pushing hard at exercise, try ‘slow jogging’

Avid runners are often chasing speed. Whether that’s improving their 5K or shaving seconds off their marathon time to nail a personal best. The idea that exercise should involve pushing further, harder or faster has long been embedded in fitness culture.

But against this backdrop, some people have adopted the almost counter-cultural belief that the key to fitness is to take things slow.

The growing popularity of the “slow jogging” trend online counters a lot of what we’ve been taught about fitness. Rather than striving for speed, the slow jogging trend encourages people to take short steps and move at a pace slow enough to comfortably hold a conversation.

To some people, this might look too easy to count as exercise. But exercise does not have to be intense to improve health.

The slow jogging trend was originally developed by a Japanese researcher named Hiroaki Tanaka. The trend eventually caught on in South Korea before going viral online, where it is now being adopted by people all around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Marlon James’s 2026 novel, The Disappearers, has already been hailed as the novel of the century by The New York Times, and it is certainly magnificent and explosive in equal measure. Its success lies in the way its artistic execution dovetails with its highly charged subject matter.

The Disappearers pulls the reader into a seemingly knowable time and place – the Jamaica of 1988 to 2005. Yet what James seeks to make known and felt is not to be found in any record or archive. Focusing on the experiences of men who love, desire, and have sex with men in a virulently homophobic Jamaican society, this is a novel that explores a silenced history with astonishing depth and detail.

In my own work, I have published literary criticism that argues for the Caribbean as a constitutively queer, as well as a homophobic, space and I found The Disappearers to be a powerful literary reckoning with this hidden past. It strives to bear witness to the harm done to young and old men, with the damage inflicted on masculinity, with the volatile entanglements of vulnerability and exploitation, and with the ferocity and survival of queer intimacy. item.title: A gallery of memories: How Kolkata’s citizens are preserving the city’s Chinese heritage
item.description: The Cheenapara Heritage Gallery in Tiretta Bazar is part of an urban revival initiative that also aims to revive the Chinese neighbourhood’s food streets.
item.content:encoded:
A menu from the 1960s from Waldorf Restaurant, located on Russell Street. A bottle of Pou Chong’s sauce, established in a factory in Tangra.

These are among the artefacts on display at the Cheenapara Heritage Gallery, which opened its doors in Kolkata’s Tiretta Bazar on September 5 to showcase the rich heritage of the city’s Chinese community.

“We need a place to keep, preserve, document, and showcase all of it to not just the Chinese community but also Kolkata’s citizens at large,” said Sohini Pyne, a conservation architect and curator of the gallery. “Those who live in Kolkata must know the Chinese history of the city and the intimate stories of these spaces.”

Added Chen Yao Hua, the gallery’s manager, “It is also a way to honour our ancestors who worked so hard to make a home in this city.”

A city of Chinatowns

item.title: ‘Good Arguments’: Playwright Deepika Arwind’s first novel for adults is fresh and fiercely feminist
item.description: The novel captures the essence of being a young woman trying to build a life in the arts while learning to navigate newly discovered adult worlds.
item.content:encoded:
Deepika Arwind’s Good Arguments is an ambitious work of fiction that captures the multitudinous realities of women living in urban spaces in India. Through the story of the protagonist, 20-something Delphi Rodriguez, Arwind captures the essence of being a young woman trying to build a life in the arts while learning to navigate newly discovered adult worlds. Set in the early 2010s, the novel follows Delphi as she begins to forge her own identity while attempting to decode the theatre scene in Bangalore, a space in which both her class and her gender make her an outsider.

Delphi is freshly out of college when she lands a role in an intensive theatre training programme run by Laila, a renowned director in the theatre community. item.title: Maharashtra declares drought in 74% of the state
item.description: The government ordered the administration to assess the damage to crops and undertake relief measures in 265 of the state’s 358 subdistricts.
item.content:encoded:
The Maharashtra government on Saturday declared drought conditions in 74% of the state’s subdistricts amid a deficit in rainfall during the southwest monsoon season.

The government order facilitates the assessment of crop damage and enables 12 relief measures including a waiver of land revenue, restructuring of crop loans, a stay on the recovery of farm loans, concession on electricity bills of agricultural pumps, and making available tankers to supply drinking water.

The order covers 265 of the state’s 358 talukas where a “trigger-1” criterion has been met. The 2026 Drought Management Code defines trigger-1 as a dry spell of at least 21 consecutive days during the monsoon.

The affected talukas are spread across 32 of the state’s 34 districts including Ahilyanagar, Amravati, Beed, Bhandara, Gadchiroli, Jalgaon, Latur, Nagpur, Nanded, Nandurbar, Parbhani, Pune, Ratnagiri, Sangli, Sindhudurg, Solapur, Wardha and Yavatmal.

The southwest monsoon is expected to begin its withdrawal from Maharashtra by October 5 with a 17% rainfall deficit, The Indian Express reported. The average deficit at the national level is 15%.

Between June 1 and September 22, Maharashtra recorded an average 787.2 mm of rainfall against the usual average of 953.2 mm during the period. In Solapur district, the rainfall was 57% below normal, The Indian Express reported. In Ahilyanagar, the deficit was 42%, followed by 34% in...

item.title: What fish can teach us about AI: Reflections on reading ‘What a Fish Knows’ alongside ‘Scary Smart
item.description: The two books tackle a common concern: how do we respond when we encounter a form of intelligence that is not a mirror of our own?
item.content:encoded:
Having worked extensively with small-scale fishing communities around the world, I am acutely aware of fishers’ perspectives about the fish they harvest. They train themselves to perceive the way fish think, feel, and know. All this is key to a successful harvest. Fishers educated me to think about fish not merely as a natural resource.

Knowing my interest in fishers and fish, a friend recently presented me with a book I would never otherwise have discovered – What a Fish Knows: The Inner Lives of Our Underwater Cousins by Jonathan Balcombe.

More recently, I stumbled across Scary Smart: The Future of Artificial Intelligence and How You Can Save Our World by Mo Gawdat. It’s the latest of books I’ve read because I’ve been curious about predictions that this technology will dominate our futures. In Scary Smart, the Egyptian author and former technology executive Gawdat took me step by step towards a different understanding of AI – what it really is, what it can become and how we might collectively shape its future.

item.description: His remarks came two days after an Indian ship crew member was killed in an attack on a commercial ship off the coast of Oman.
item.content:encoded:
Union Minister S Jaishankar on Friday said that attacks on seafarers and commercial ships were “regrettably” no longer exceptional occurrences and the loss of lives was “indefensible”, PTI reported.

His remarks came two days after an Indian seafarer was killed in an attack on a commercial ship off the coast of Oman. It was the 11th death of an Indian ship crew member in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in West Asia began.

The external affairs minister’s remarks also came on the day India and Liberia announced the establishment of a “group of friends” on the safety and security of shipping and seafarers on the sidelines of the 80th United Nations General Assembly.

“In the last few months, commercial shipping and mariners have been subjected to repeated attacks in the Gulf, the Red Sea and its vicinity,” PTI quoted Jaishankar as saying. “These actions that disrupt maritime commerce and cost innocent lives are simply indefensible.”

He added: “India, as a major source of seafarers, and Liberia, as the largest shipping registry, have come together to highlight the safety and security of shipping and seafarers.”

item.title: How Krishna Bisht crossed Delhi’s cultural divide to carry the Dilli gharana into a new era
item.description: A disciple of Chand Khan, Bisht became a leading practitioner and scholar of a gharana long shaped by male hereditary musicians.
item.content:encoded:
The distance between Mausiqi Manzil in Daryaganj and the small, manicured bungalows on Rouse Avenue near ITO was not great. But in the Delhi of the 1950s, entire worlds separated the lives of Chand Khan and Krishna Chakravarty. He was the khalifa or steward of the Dilli Gharana, a strictly patriarchal lineage of hereditary Muslim musicians entrenched in the chaos of the old city. She came from an equally conservative family of Vaishnavite Bengalis, immersed in notions of ritual purity, in central Delhi. But come together they did, as guru and shishya, forging a decades-long relationship built on music.

The ustad died in 1980, and his nephew, the late Iqbal Khan, was to inherit the gharana mantle. But today, Krishna Bisht, 82, is considered the senior-most representative of a musical tradition that claims to trace its origin to the times of Amir Khusrau. Over the intervening decades, she also forged a style for women singers in a gharana that had been tailored for masculine vigour.

item.title: A prestigious documentary festival in Keralam is in censorship limbo
item.description: These titles explore the issues that matter in India and the rest of the world.
item.content:encoded:
Another film event, another instance of censorship. This time, it’s the turn of the International Documentary & Short Films Festival of Keralam.

This year’s edition, which kicked off on Friday in Thiruvananthapuram, was barred by the Information Broadcasting Ministry from showing 31 pre-selected titles, according to reports.

These include Spandan Banerjee’s Parliament Street, Shimmering Odyssey by Prasun Goswami and Raunak Shivhare, Sanitised Republic: Cast(e) & Contracts by Afiya Khalid and Rizwan Rahman, Saranyya Deyy’s In Search of Buddha, Sepideh Farsi’s Put Your Soul on Your Hand and Walk and Memories of a Window by Amin Pakparvar and Mehraneh Salimian.

These titles explore the issues that matter in India and the rest of the world – caste, revolutionary movements, education in conflict zones, workers’ rights, the Gaza genocide. They also run contrary to the shiny rhetoric peddled by the Bharatiya Janata Party-led government in Delhi.

In a note sent to filmmakers, the festival organisers wrote, “We regret to inform you that, as we have not received the necessary censor exemption for your film from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, we will be unable to screen it at the 18th IDSFFK.”

item.title: ‘I was interested in writing a character who believes in the reality of the dreamworld’: Avni Doshi
item.description: An interview with Doshi about her new novel, ‘The First House.’
item.content:encoded:
The First House begins with the end of a marriage. Avni Doshi does it coldly, almost unsentimentally – watching the ambush like a guerrilla leader who has been planning it all her life.

The new novel comes six years after Burnt Sugar was published and shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

Doshi does not like smooth, open roads without milestones. Navigating the unexpected is her territory. In her second and latest novel, amidst trusted spaces and ambiguity in time, astrology and myth, an inevitable lesson comes forth: There is no one story, no single sentence. Her men are constantly under surveillance in the women’s gaze. In this book, omens are real.

Writing the final drafts in Dubai, far from India, she says she carries places inside her.

In this conversation with Scroll, sometimes guided by geometrical precision and at times punctuated by silences, Doshi talks about listening to a voice like a river, and why control is the real delusion, and why she does not feel the pressure to please anyone with her writing. item.title: Ramachandra Guha’s new book: Gandhi’s nonviolence prepared Indians to use their freedom responsibly
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Arguments with Gandhi’.
item.content:encoded:
In the past, the argument that Gandhi’s reliance on non-violence delayed the country’s freedom from British rule was put forward most insistently by Marxists, themselves enchanted with the examples of Lenin and Mao. More recently, the ideas that non-violence was a bogus and ineffective strategy has become widespread among Indians who are not remotely attached to Marxism. Those who argue that the struggle against British rule should have relied largely or exclusively on violence make two claims – first, that freedom would then have come sooner than 1947; and second, that a legacy of successful armed struggle against colonialism would have led to a more realistic, hard-headed, and effective foreign policy for the nation once it was independent. Gandhi, and the Gandhian legacy, are charged with weakening the Indian people in their fight against Western imperialism as well as with undermining the Indian nation’s ability to become a major player in global affairs.

The Tamil novelist and public intellectual D Jeyamohan has persuasively challenged the belief that violent revolution would have led the British to depart sooner, or resulted in a better and stronger India. item.title: ‘The leaves tremble to your tune’: These poems ask enduring questions about mortality and meaning
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Two Pits: New and Selected Poems’, by Siddhartha Menon.
item.content:encoded:
Playtime

And what do we foretell
of the kids beneath these high windows?
Through all the goings on a stab
right out of Bruegel’s Children’s Games:
“Can I play with you?” and feet
after a painted tyre
faltering: “Let me also play…?”
The world has come to a standstill.
The evening birds that oversee the play-space
are silenced. Like psephologists
at the time of a big verdict
we glance obliquely at a cluttered scene
and smile uncertainty aside.


Fat Cat

This cat is low-slung
with a belly full of bombs.
It was beneath the car
and has made it to the undergrowth
where all you see is a tail twitching
as if it were a tiger.
But this is no make believe:
its payload is real
and deadly. A matter of moments
in wariness
for populations to explode.


To A Rich Young Girl

It feels so good to her
the tug on her waist-length hair
being brushed as she stands in the garden
her eyes shut to the early
filter of sun as her head
is gently rocked with each
downward stroke it feels
so good
and with translucence
warming her eyelids and birdsong
turning on the sky
the universe is hers
to toy with where she stands.


The Pencil

Prospectives prowl the corridor
to sniff out whether one day that towel askew
could be their child’s.

They are meeting here for the first time
like tourists on a conducted tour
in a coach with meshed windows.

Their voices merge then separate
tinged with nervous wonder...

item.title: Never mind the sunglasses. Nepal’s Balen Shah gives the UN a powerful argument about climate justice
item.description: He proposed a ‘Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism’ that would bring Nepal, India and China together to share scientific information and disaster warnings.

There are better ways to spend the early hours of a Friday morning than waiting in Dhaka for a prime minister to speak in New York. Journalism, unfortunately, does not always offer them.

I was on the graveyard shift, waiting for Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s maiden address to the United Nations General Assembly. My calculation put him at the lectern at around 4.30 am Dhaka time. So I did what journalists do while waiting for history to happen: I scrolled through the programme and listened to other people making history instead.

Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley was speaking – eloquent and considerably more effective than the average United Nations address, a genre in which 15 minutes can occasionally feel like a geological era.

Then I noticed a familiar name farther down the speakers’ list: Balendra “Balen” Shah, the 36-year-old prime minister of Nepal. That was enough to keep me awake.

Nepal is one of my favourite countries and, as an avid trekker, one I have visited repeatedly. But there was another, admittedly less statesmanlike, reason for staying up. I wanted to know whether the rapper-turned-mayor-turned-prime-minister would actually address the United Nations wearing his trademark black sunglasses.

He did. Of course he did.

item.description: Nearly six months later, many are still in jail.
item.content:encoded:
In April, the energy crisis triggered by the conflict in West Asia ate into the meagre incomes of working-class Indians, precipitating a cost-of-living crisis for many of them. Thousands of workers hit the streets in Noida, an industrial city in the National Capital Region, to demand an increase in their minimum wage, which had not been revised since 2014.

The government of Uttar Pradesh responded by detaining hundreds of protesters, some of whom have spent months in jail.

This is the story of three such women – a factory worker who doubled up as an activist, a domestic worker who was inspired by the workers to demand better working conditions for herself, and an artist who joined the protests in solidarity.

Two out of these three women remain behind bars because the police have filed nearly a dozen cases against them for allegedly inciting violence during the agitation. Scroll made several visits to Noida to piece together this account of their lives.

Get it? F-L-Y-I-N-G!

item.title: J&K: BJP protests Omar Abdullah’s statehood resolution
item.description: Bharatiya Janata Party MLAs objected to a reference to the 2000 autonomy resolution in the new one.
item.content:encoded:
Bharatiya Janata Party MLAs in Jammu and Kashmir on Friday protested against a reference to a 2000 autonomy resolution made in a fresh one moved by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah seeking statehood for the Union Territory, The Telegraph reported.

The text of the fresh resolution moved by Abdullah on Friday says that in addition to the resolutions passed by the Assembly in June 2000 and November 2024, the House was calling on the Union government to urgently restore Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood.

In June 2000, the National Conference government led by Farooq Abdullah passed a resolution in the Assembly calling for restoration of greater autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir as it existed before August 1953. However, it was rejected by the then-Atal Bihari Vajpayee government at the Centre.

In November 2024, the Assembly passed another resolution calling for the restoration of the special status the erstwhile state had under Article 370 of the Constitution, which was abrogated by the Union government in August 2019.

During the Assembly proceedings on Friday, BJP MLAs entered the well of the House and tore copies of the resolution following the reference to the 2000 resolution, The Telegraph reported.

The speaker adjourned the proceedings for the day after a scuffle between legislators.

The Nehru Park area has several embassies and diplomatic missions.

The BSF teams began patrolling the park at 4 pm and were ordered to remain there until 10 pm, the newspaper quoted an unidentified official as saying. Police officers were also patrolling the park.

“This park gets many visitors, especially foreigners,” the official was quoted as saying. “You can always see vehicles of different embassy officials at two parking lots. If anything happens here, it will be all over the news.”

The park has at least 11 entry gates but only five private male security guards and one female guard, the newspaper reported.

The BSF is primarily responsible for guarding India’s borders with Pakistan and Bangladesh. It is also deployed for internal security in anti-terror operations.

item.title: Gaza genocide allegations ‘greatest lie of the century’, claims Benjamin Netanyahu
item.description: The remark came even as an independent United Nations inquiry panel stated in September 2025 that Tel Aviv had committed genocide against Palestinians.
item.content:encoded:
The allegations of Israel having committed a genocide in Gaza is the “greatest lie of the century”, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.

Netanyahu quoted urban warfare expert United States Colonel John Spencer (retired) as having said that Israel “has done more to prevent civilian casualties in war than any other military in history”.

The Israeli military had taken “innumerable steps to protect” civilians, Netanyahu claimed. “Is this genocide?” he asked. “Of course not. It’s the opposite of genocide.”

Netanyahu’s claims contradict growing consensus among international organisations, governments and human rights bodies that the Israeli military’s actions in the besieged Palestinian territory amount to a genocide.

Israel has carried out unprecedented air and ground strikes on Gaza, leaving more than 73,900 persons dead. The Israeli military’s offensive in Gaza had begun in October 2023 after the Palestinian militant group Hamas killed 1,200 persons during its incursion into southern Israel and took hostages.

While heavy fighting has largely paused since October 2025 following a ceasefire between Tel Aviv and Hamas, much of Gaza remains under Israeli military control.

A United States Panel on religious freedom on Thursday accused India of “weaponising” the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act to detain religious minorities, including activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, who remain jailed in pre-trial detention, for “simply engaging in peaceful protests”.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom also urged Washington’s Department of State to work with the Indian authorities to facilitate the release of other “freedom of religion or belief” prisoners.

New Delhi is yet to comment on this statement.

Khalid and Imam have been in judicial custody for six years in connection with the conspiracy case related to the 2020 Delhi riots. The trial in the case is yet to begin.

The US panel defines “freedom of religion or belief” prisoners as individuals who are jailed, detained, or placed in confinement by governments primarily because of their religious faith, peaceful worship, or expression of personal beliefs.

Tamil director Karthik Subbaraj’s Dorothy is set in 1995, in a village in Madurai where caste lines are thickly drawn, family honour is paramount and ascribed roles are rejected only on pain of death. The equation between Subbu and Karthi is forged in a cauldron of moustache-twirling masculinity.

Subbu (Sananth), the son of the moneylender Veeraiya (Muthukumar), and Karthi (Rishikanth) becomes fast friends despite differences in caste and social status. The foundation of the bond that begins in childhood and endures into adulthood includes a love for movies and Bruce Lee fandom.

Subbu is the martial arts expert as a child, saving Karthi from bullies. Boys never cry, Subbu keeps telling Karthi.

Nothing can possibly come between us, the buddies shrug. A mutual acquaintance laughs in response, having seen more of the world than these young men.

That something has the force of a tsunami, destroying all that Subbu and Karthi hold dear. In a typical film, that something is usually embodied by a woman, who can be relied on drive a wedge between best friends.

Dorothy (Keerthy Suresh) enters Subbu’s household as his sister-in-law and charms both Subbu and Karthi. Dorothy doesn’t only have an unusual name.

item.title: Tishani Doshi’s poetry collection ‘Egrets, While War’ is shortlisted for the 2026 PEN Heaney Prize
item.description: The winner will be announced on December 1.
item.content:encoded:
Indian poet Tishani Doshi’s latest book, Egrets, While War, is shortlisted for the 2026 PEN Heaney Prize.

The prize, instituted in 2024, recognises a single volume of poetry by one author, published in the UK or Ireland, of outstanding literary merit that engages with the impact of cultural or political events on human conditions or relationships. It is open to both original English language collections and those translated into English.

This year’s jury comprises poets Victoria Adukwei Bulley, Vona Groarke and Stephen Sexton.

“Tishani Doshi’s dextrous, vibrant and vital poems delight and shimmer. Across Egrets, While War, the range of her subjects is vast: the ancient and modern co-mingle with poems of personal and civic responsibility,” said the jury. “Throughout, an aviary of sonnets addresses the birds of mythology and literature with grace and invention. Wars, historical and contemporary, provide the contexts for these powerful poems of resistance and humanity.”

The winner will be announced on December 1.

item.title: Assembly polls: BJP spent more in Bengal than Congress did in four states, one UT
item.description: The Bharatiya Janata Party’s expenditure in West Bengal was more than half of its total spending in all five elections.
item.content:encoded:
The Bharatiya Janata Party spent Rs 286.9 crore on the West Bengal election, more than the Rs 248.5 crore the Congress spent in all five Assembly polls held this year, the parties’ expenditure statements filed with the Election Commission showed.

In 2026, Assembly elections were held in Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Puducherry.

The BJP spent Rs 529.3 crore on the Assembly polls in four states and one Union Territory.

The Hindutva party’s expenditure in West Bengal was more than half of its total spending in all five elections, the data showed.

The BJP won 207 seats in the 294-member Assembly, ending the 15-year rule of the Trinamool Congress.

The expenditure filings made by the Trinamool Congress have not been made public yet.

The Congress spent Rs 42 crore in West Bengal. The party had won two seats in the state.

While there are limits on how much a candidate can spend on contesting elections, parties can spend an unlimited amount on fighting polls. After each election, parties are required to submit a detailed account of the expenses incurred, which includes spending on travel, rallies, advertisements and campaign materials.

item.title: No ‘paneer’ tag for analogue products, FSSAI proposes
item.description: Analogue paneer is a non-dairy or partially synthetic substitute that replaces milk fat and milk solids with cheaper vegetable oils.
item.content:encoded:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has proposed restricting the manufacture and sale of analogue products as “paneer” to prevent consumers from being misled about their nature and composition.

Analogue paneer is a non-dairy or partially synthetic substitute that replaces milk fat and milk solids with cheaper vegetable oils, making it cheaper to produce than dairy paneer.

The food regulator’s draft notification, issued on Tuesday, proposes barring products in the “analogue in dairy context” category from using the term “paneer” in their name, labels or marketing.

The regulator has invited public feedback on the draft within 60 days of its publication.

In recent months, several states including Maharashtra, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana, Himachal Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh have banned the production and sale of analogue paneer, citing public health concerns.

item.title: Delhi court allows US citizen, six Ukrainians held by NIA to visit families abroad for a month
item.description: The seven foreigners were arrested in March for allegedly having links to ethnic armed groups in Myanmar that are hostile to India.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi court on Thursday permitted a United States citizen and six Ukrainians, who were arrested by the National Investigation Agency in March for allegedly having links to ethnic armed groups in Myanmar that are hostile to India, to travel to their respective countries for a month, The Hindu reported.

The US citizen, Matthew Aaron Van Dyke, and the six Ukrainians were arrested on March 13. They were allegedly involved in supplying weapons and military equipment to ethnic armed groups operating in Myanmar, as well as providing them with training.

On September 8, the NIA filed a chargesheet against the seven foreigners for illegally entering, staying and moving in India under the 2025 Immigration and Foreigners Act.

item.title: For India’s Gen Z, being young is no longer the all-powerful force it once was
item.description: Being young in India has always meant being demographically dominant. That is changing fast.
item.content:encoded:
Student street protests in India in July 2026 forced the country to pay more attention to its Gen Z population, the cohort of young people born after 1996, who are now between the ages of 14 and 29.

This has meant confronting questions around the availability of quality education, fairness in educational processes and outcomes, and the job market squeeze. Yet simultaneously, India’s Gen Z must also confront a country where being young is no longer the all-powerful force that it once was.

End of India’s baby boom

Being young in India has always meant being demographically dominant. India belonged to its children. Since 1950, the year from which reliable internationally comparable population data is available, children have always been the largest cohort in India. If you split the population up into equally-sized cohorts, each of which spanned 15 years, the group that was the largest in size was always children – those between the ages of 0 and 14. This held true whether you looked at them in absolute numbers, or in relative terms – children were India’s largest cohort.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has framed these changes as part of a broader, “orderly” and “fair” approach to lowering net overseas migration. But they also continue a years-long push by the federal government to lower international student numbers.

What has been announced? And what is happening with international student numbers more broadly?

What did Tony Burke say?

On Thursday, Burke told the National Press Club most international students will have to come alone to Australia. There will be some exceptions, including for people from Pacific and ASEAN countries and PhD students.

Last year, more than 45,000 visas were granted to family members of an international student.

item.title: Wendell Berry spent his life farming, writing. His legacy is an ethic of care for the natural world
item.description: Caring for the planet, the poet believed, means recognising your own place in it. He died on August 31, aged 92.
item.content:encoded:
The American farmer, novelist and poet Wendell Berry, died on August 31, aged 92. Berry farmed in Port Royal, in his native Kentucky, for over 40 years. Through his writing and his farming, Berry emphasised the importance of both community and care for the planet, advocating for small-scale agriculture as key to both.

He criticised modern consumer culture, suggesting, in his poem Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front, that instead of buying into the rat race, people should: “Love the world. Work for nothing […] / Say that your main crop is the forests / that you did not plant / that you will not live to harvest.”

His prolific output included The Unsettling of America: Culture and Agriculture (1977), Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer (1987) and The Mad Farmer Poems (2008).

Caring for the planet, Berry believed, means recognising your own place in it. Not as the centre, but as part of a wider community of interconnected life. In doing so, Berry’s writing highlights an important new theme in environmental humanities: a growing interest in “georgic” writing as an environmental genre.

What can a Jain merchant family in Mughal Ahmedabad tell us about doing business in India, both in the past and the present?

Quite a lot, as Sudev Sheth explains in this episode of Past Imperfect. Sheth is the author of Bankrolling Empire, the captivating story of how one business family, the Jhaveris of Ahmedabad, navigated the highs and lows of commercial life under Mughal suzerainty.

Although firmly enmeshed in the worlds of 17th- and 18th-century India, the Jhaveris faced challenges that any modern Indian business family can relate to. They reaped enormous benefits from close ties to the government – but also suffered when they got on the wrong side of certain officials.
